Title: This file uses an older character encoding ({encoding})
Meaning: Most programs today expect UTF-8. Some will show accented letters wrongly when they import this file.
HowToFix: Download the repaired file below, which is converted to UTF-8. Or, when you export from your program, pick "UTF-8" as the character set.

Title: The file says it's {declared}, but it's really {encoding}
Meaning: The header names one character set, but the letters in the file are written in another. A program that trusts the header will show accented letters as gibberish.
HowToFix: Download the repaired file below. Its header matches its contents.

Title: The file doesn't say which character set it uses
Meaning: We read it as UTF-8. Another program might guess differently.
HowToFix: Download the repaired file below, which says UTF-8 in its header.

Title: {count} characters couldn't be read
Meaning: These bytes don't match any letter in the file's character set. They show as � here. The letters were probably damaged before this file was made.
HowToFix: Find these people in your program and retype the names or places shown with �.

Title: Some characters were in a different encoding
Meaning: {count} characters were in a different encoding from the rest of the file. We've read them as best we can — check the names and places on these lines.
HowToFix: Look at the names and places on these lines in your program and correct any letter that looks wrong. The repaired file keeps the letters as we read them.

Title: A line is longer than GEDCOM allows
Meaning: GEDCOM lines may be at most 255 characters. Some programs cut longer lines short and lose the end of the text.
HowToFix: The repaired file splits long notes into continuation lines. For other kinds of line, shorten the text in your program.

Title: A line is longer than GEDCOM allows
Meaning: GEDCOM lines may be at most 255 characters. Some programs cut longer lines short and lose the end of the text.
HowToFix: The repaired file splits long notes into continuation lines. For other kinds of line, shorten the text in your program.

Title: Blank line
Meaning: GEDCOM files shouldn't have blank lines. Most programs skip them, but a few stop reading.
HowToFix: The repaired file removes them.

Title: A line starts with spaces
Meaning: Every line should start with its level number. Some programs reject lines that start with a space.
HowToFix: The repaired file removes the spaces.

Title: A line we couldn't read
Meaning: Every line needs a level number and a tag, like `1 NAME`. This one doesn't, so we skipped it. Anything it held is missing from the check.
HowToFix: Open the file in a text editor at this line and see what it should be. The most common cause is a note whose text runs onto a new line without a `CONT` tag.

Title: A line's level number isn't a number
Meaning: Every line starts with a number that shows how it nests under the line above. We skipped this line.
HowToFix: Usually a note whose text broke onto a new line. Fix it in a text editor, or re-export from your program.

Title: A record has an id but no type
Meaning: This line has an id like `@I1@` but doesn't say whether it is a person, a family or something else. We skipped it.
HowToFix: Re-export from your program. If it happens again, tell the program's makers.

Title: Lines nest too deeply
Meaning: This line is nested more than 100 levels deep, which no real file needs. The file is probably damaged.
HowToFix: Re-export from your program.

Title: A line skips a level
Meaning: This line is nested two or more levels below the line above it. Programs may attach it to the wrong thing or drop it.
HowToFix: Find this person or family in your program and check the event or fact near this line. If it looks right there, re-export.

Title: There's text before the file's header
Meaning: A GEDCOM file must begin with `0 HEAD`. We ignored {count} lines before it.
HowToFix: Open the file in a text editor and delete everything above `0 HEAD`, or re-export from your program.

Title: A kind of record we don't read
Meaning: Your program saved some of its own records here (`{tag}`). Other programs usually ignore them. Nothing is wrong with your tree.
HowToFix: Nothing to do, unless you need this information in another program.

Title: The file has no header
Meaning: A GEDCOM file must start with `0 HEAD`. Without it, most programs won't open the file.
HowToFix: Re-export from your program.

Title: The file has no end marker
Meaning: A GEDCOM file should end with `0 TRLR`. Without it, the file may have been cut short while it was copied or downloaded.
HowToFix: Check that the file's last people are all there. The repaired file adds the end marker.

Title: We couldn't read the whole file
Meaning: Something stopped us reading the file to the end. It may be damaged, or it may not be a GEDCOM file.
HowToFix: Export the file from your program again and check the new copy.

Title: The file doesn't say who made it
Meaning: GEDCOM {gedcom_version} expects the header to name a submitter, meaning the person who made the file. Most programs don't mind.
HowToFix: In your program, fill in your name as the researcher or submitter, then export again.

Title: An id is longer than this GEDCOM version allows
Meaning: Ids like `@I123@` may be at most 20 characters in GEDCOM before 7.0. Some programs reject longer ones.
HowToFix: Usually nothing you can change in your program. If an import fails, tell the program's makers.

Title: A person has no id
Meaning: Every person needs an id such as `@I1@` so families can point to them. Nothing can link to this person.
HowToFix: Re-export from your program.

Title: A family has no id
Meaning: Every family needs an id such as `@F1@` so people can point to it.
HowToFix: Re-export from your program.

Title: {person} is a child of a family that doesn't exist
Meaning: The file links {person} to family {target} as a child, but there's no such family in the file. The link is lost on import.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and check their parents. Remove the broken link and add the parents again.

Title: {person} is a spouse in a family that doesn't exist
Meaning: The file links {person} to family {target} as a partner, but there's no such family.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and check their spouses or partners.

Title: A family's husband doesn't exist
Meaning: Family {family} names {target} as husband, but there's no such person in the file.
HowToFix: Open the family in your program and choose the husband again.

Title: A family's wife doesn't exist
Meaning: Family {family} names {target} as wife, but there's no such person in the file.
HowToFix: Open the family in your program and choose the wife again.

Title: A family's child doesn't exist
Meaning: Family {family} lists {target} as a child, but there's no such person in the file.
HowToFix: Open the family in your program and check its children.

Title: A source that doesn't exist
Meaning: {person} cites source {target}, but there's no such source in the file. The citation is lost on import.
HowToFix: Open the citation in your program and choose the source again.

Title: A note that doesn't exist
Meaning: {person} points to note {target}, but there's no such note in the file.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and check their notes.

Title: A link to something that doesn't exist
Meaning: A `{pointer_tag}` line points to {target}, but there's no such record in the file.
HowToFix: Find the record at this line in your program and remove or redo the link.

Title: An association with no person
Meaning: {person} has an association (godparent, witness and so on) that doesn't say who with.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and fix or remove the association.

Title: An association with someone who doesn't exist
Meaning: {person} is associated with {target}, but there's no such person in the file.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and fix or remove the association.

Title: An association that doesn't point to a person
Meaning: {person}'s association points to {target}, which is a {target_tag}, not a person.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and choose the associated person again.

Title: An association that doesn't say what the relationship is
Meaning: {person} is associated with {target} but the file doesn't say how, for example godparent or witness.
HowToFix: Open the association in your program and fill in the relationship.

Title: A family with nobody in it
Meaning: This family has no husband, wife or children. It's usually left over from deleting people.
HowToFix: Find the empty family in your program and delete it.

Title: {person} died before they were born
Meaning: Death year {death_year} is before birth year {birth_year}. One of the dates is probably mistyped.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and check both dates against your sources.

Title: {person} lived to {age}
Meaning: Possible, but rare. Often a typo in a year, or two people with the same name combined into one.
HowToFix: Check {person}'s birth and death dates against your sources.

Title: {person} was baptised before they were born
Meaning: Baptism ({bapm}) is before birth ({birt}).
HowToFix: Check both dates. Sometimes the baptism date was entered as the birth date.

Title: {person} was buried before they died
Meaning: Burial ({buri}) is before death ({deat}).
HowToFix: Check both dates against your sources.

Title: {child} was born before their father
Meaning: {child} was born before {father}. Usually a mistyped year, or the child linked to the wrong family.
HowToFix: Check both birth dates, and that {child} is in the right family.

Title: {child} was born before their mother
Meaning: {child} was born before {mother}. Usually a mistyped year, or the child linked to the wrong family.
HowToFix: Check both birth dates, and that {child} is in the right family.

Title: {father} was {age} when {child} was born
Meaning: That's younger than usual for a father. It may be right, but it's often a typo or the wrong family.
HowToFix: Check both birth dates and {child}'s parents.

Title: {mother} was {age} when {child} was born
Meaning: That's younger than usual for a mother. It may be right, but it's often a typo or the wrong family.
HowToFix: Check both birth dates and {child}'s parents.

Title: {father} was {age} when {child} was born
Meaning: That's older than usual for a father. It's often two men with the same name combined into one.
HowToFix: Check both birth dates and {child}'s parents.

Title: {mother} was {age} when {child} was born
Meaning: That's well past the age women usually have children. It's often a typo or the wrong family.
HowToFix: Check both birth dates and {child}'s parents.

Title: {person} married before they were born
Meaning: The marriage in {marriage_year} is before {person}'s birth.
HowToFix: Check the marriage date and {person}'s birth date.

Title: {person} married at {age}
Meaning: That's younger than usual. It may be right for the time and place, or a mistyped year.
HowToFix: Check the marriage date and {person}'s birth date.

Title: A date we couldn't understand
Meaning: {person}'s {event} date reads "{date}". Programs may ignore it or read it differently.
HowToFix: Rewrite it as a GEDCOM date, such as `12 MAR 1850`, `ABT 1850`, `BEF 1850` or `BET 1850 AND 1855`. Free text belongs in a note.

Title: The husband and wife may be swapped
Meaning: In this family, the person entered as husband is female and the person entered as wife is male.
HowToFix: Open the family in your program and check who is in which place, and each person's sex.

Title: A person with no name
Meaning: Person {person} has no name in the file. They'll show as "unknown" in most programs.
HowToFix: Open the person in your program and add a name, even a partial one.

Title: A name that's blank
Meaning: {person} has a name line with nothing in it.
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and fill in or remove the empty name.

Title: We can't tell which part of the name is the surname
Meaning: GEDCOM marks the surname with slashes, as in `John /Smith/`. This name has none, so other programs may sort it wrongly.
HowToFix: In your program, put the surname in the surname field. If the person has no known surname, this is fine.

Title: A sex value other programs won't understand
Meaning: {person}'s sex is "{sex}". GEDCOM allows M, F, U (unknown), X (intersex) and N (not recorded).
HowToFix: Open {person} in your program and choose their sex again.
